name: Jesse Ventura
role: Governor of Minnesota (1999-2003); former professional wrestler and actor
summary: As governor of Minnesota, Ventura pushed for a single-chamber legislature and vetoed new abortion restrictions. After leaving office he campaigned against a constitutional ban on same-sex marriage, criticized the Iraq invasion and post-September 11 restrictions on civil liberties, and advocated cannabis legalization.

abortion-legal.rationale: Ventura vetoed the 2000 abortion informed-consent bill, which required a waiting period and new conditions before most abortions.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: Ventura told Larry King that faith communities can often do a better job than government at welfare and helping people.

civil-marriage.rationale: Ventura distinguished civil marriage from religious recognition and insisted that officials issue same-sex marriage licenses regardless of their own religious beliefs.

collective-bargaining.rationale: During the 1998 gubernatorial debate, Ventura endorsed collective bargaining and urged the parties to the Northwest Airlines dispute to stay at the bargaining table.

conscription.rationale: In 2009 Ventura explicitly reversed his earlier opposition to the draft. He repeated his support in a later interview, calling for medical grounds to be the only deferment.

corporate-influence.rationale: In “The Wall Street Conspiracy,” Ventura points to insurance lobbying against health reform and to the influence of finance-industry lobbyists and executives over the response to the banking crisis.

cut-consumption-tax.rationale: Ventura’s 2001 tax reform address calls for keeping food, clothing and heating fuels exempt from the sales tax.

death-penalty.rationale: In 2002 Ventura expressly opposed execution and said a life sentence should mean life in prison.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: In the election-fraud chapter of American Conspiracies, Ventura calls for abolishing the Electoral College and deciding presidential elections by the popular vote.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Ventura’s Alaska candidate statement calls for a major national effort on climate, and in his Here & Now interview he condemned US withdrawal from the Paris Agreement.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: In “Subverting the Constitution,” Ventura rejects a Justice Department memo that treated terrorism as grounds for setting aside ordinary constitutional protections.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Ventura said that everyone should be equal under the law and that government’s role is to meet common needs on an equal footing.

foreign-policy-non-interference.rationale: Ventura describes imposing American beliefs abroad as imperialism and calls for closing the overseas bases and bringing US troops home.

free-public-college.rationale: Ventura argued that students should use lower-cost community college and part-time work to pay their own way through college.

government-encourage-intercultural-conta.rationale: Ventura called for government leadership on contact across racial and cultural groups, and described a Department of Human Rights initiative to engage local councils and residents.

harm-principle.rationale: In “Your Government Dealing Drugs,” Ventura rejects criminal penalties for harm to oneself and argues that individuals should decide what is good for them.

in-work-tax-credits.rationale: Ventura signed the 2001 special-session tax bill amending Minnesota’s refundable Working Family Credit, which supplements earnings and phases out as family income rises.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Ventura told Larry King that religious groups should not use government to legislate beliefs they had failed to persuade people to adopt.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: In his 2008 Larry King interview Ventura objects to criminalizing a consensual sexual act on the basis that adults exchanged payment.

limit-guns.rationale: In the 1998 campaign interview Ventura favored enforcing existing gun laws with restrictions for convicted felons and accepted a waiting period, while rejecting calls for further general restrictions.

national-mission.rationale: Ventura criticized using overseas military power to impose American beliefs on other countries.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Ventura’s administration implemented publicly funded transport and human-services programs under the Big Plan.

no-bailouts.rationale: Ventura said in office that the state should not guarantee that private businesses succeed. In “The Wall Street Conspiracy,” he endorses ending taxpayer guarantees for specific banks and letting insolvent banks go bankrupt.

no-business-privileges.rationale: In “The Wall Street Conspiracy,” Ventura calls for ending government handouts and guarantees that give selected large banks an advantage over their competitors.

no-central-bank.rationale: Ventura argued that the Federal Reserve was unconstitutional and that concentrating money issuance in the hands of its bankers gave them excessive power.

one-party-rule.rationale: Ventura called for eliminating the role of political parties in government altogether, including the two established parties.

open-lgbt-military-service.rationale: Ventura told Larry King that gay Americans should be allowed to serve and that he would thank them for serving their country.

party-controls-media.rationale: In the concluding chapter of American Conspiracies, Ventura criticizes the administration for paying journalists to promote its line and argues for independent investigative reporting.

patriotic-education.rationale: Ventura vetoed HF2598, which mandated public-school recitation of the Pledge of Allegiance and instruction in respect for the flag.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Ventura argues that both major parties have corrupted government and that a new party would need to adopt their practices to compete.

political-violence-legitimate.rationale: When asked about his call for a political revolution, Ventura explicitly rejected violence as a means of ending the two-party system.

public-access-to-information.rationale: In the introduction to 63 Documents, Ventura argues that government secrecy and the risks taken by people who disclose hidden records make public access to those records important.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: In his Martin Luther King Jr. Day address Ventura endorsed the goal of children of every race learning together at school, and urged adults to practice the same integration.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: In a discussion of the minimum wage, Ventura said every 40-hour job should pay enough to live without government assistance and left the calculation of the level open.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Ventura and his wife recorded and released a campaign video opposing an amendment that would bar Minnesota from recognizing same-sex marriages.

school-vouchers.rationale: In the 1998 gubernatorial debate, Ventura opposed shifting money to a private voucher system and argued for improving public schools.

second-chamber.rationale: In his 2001 State of the State address, Ventura renewed his call for a single-chamber Minnesota legislature to make lawmakers more directly accountable for their decisions.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: Ventura told Larry King that the United States should prosecute those responsible for torture, including officials up the chain of command.

separate-church-state.rationale: On Larry King Live Ventura backed separation of government and religion and said churches should not resort to legislation when they fail to persuade people.

social-market-economy.rationale: Ventura called for a balance between a capitalist economy and public services designed to give poorer people a chance to succeed.

state-arms-monopoly.rationale: Ventura publicly backed allowing civilians to qualify for concealed carry through background checks, safety training and a marksmanship test.

suppress-opposition.rationale: In the election-fraud chapter of American Conspiracies, Ventura calls for opening the ballot and debates to credible candidates outside the two major parties.

surveillance-ok.rationale: In “Subverting the Constitution,” Ventura rejects treating the threat of terrorism as a reason to set aside constitutional protection against warrantless surveillance.

term-limits.rationale: As governor Ventura proposed a constitutional amendment limiting time in office to eight years. He reaffirmed his support for term limits in 2002.

troops-home-from-abroad.rationale: Ventura criticized maintaining bases decades after wars ended and later explicitly called for bringing home the Americans stationed across the overseas base network.

unions-good.rationale: As a wrestler, Ventura tried to organize his colleagues into a union and risked losing his job over the effort.

universal-healthcare.rationale: In “The Wall Street Conspiracy,” Ventura describes treatment as a right regardless of immigration status and asks why government-run care like the veterans’ system should not be available to everyone.

notes: This pass checked the Minnesota legislative veto register, the administration’s Big Plan report, state addresses, campaign and later interview transcripts, and the local books, alongside local MediaSum transcripts. Searches on the widest uncertainty lines covered racial equality and integration, collective bargaining and income, nationalism and overseas bases, and industrial and environmental policy. The review also covered taxation and banking, elections and institutional reform, war and diplomacy, criminal justice and civil liberties, healthcare and welfare, religion and education, immigration and trade, urban growth and energy, and technology. Ventura’s early endorsement of domestic partnerships preceded his campaign against the same-sex marriage amendment. Historical citations to tertiary compilations are retained in the signed review history.
